title: SAMSON KILLED A LION WITH HIS BARE HANDS. WHEN HE RETURNED, SOMETHING IMPOSSIBLE WAS WAITING INSIDE THE CORPSE.
paragraphs: SAMSON KILLED A LION WITH HIS BARE HANDS. WHEN HE RETURNED, SOMETHING IMPOSSIBLE WAS WAITING INSIDE THE CORPSE.
The disturbing riddle of Samson, the honey hidden inside death, and the Gospel truth for anyone who thinks the ugliest chapter of their life is too ruined for God to redeem.
There was something inside the dead lion.
Something that should make you stop.
Something Samson could not have seen coming when the animal came roaring toward him.
Honey.
But before there was honey, there was a roar.
Before there was sweetness, there was violence.

Before there was a riddle told at a wedding feast, there was a private battle in a vineyard where a young man discovered that the Spirit of God could empower him to do what human strength alone could never explain.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because most of us want the honey.
We just don't want the lion.

We want resurrection without death. Restoration without devastation. Testimony without testing. A healed marriage without the night somebody almost walked away. Freedom without admitting what enslaved us. Grace without confronting sin. A new life without the death of the old one.
But Judges 14 gives us one of Scripture's strangest images.
A lion.
A carcass.
Bees.
Honey.
And a riddle nobody could solve unless they knew what Samson had survived.
The story begins with a man who was extraordinarily gifted by God and yet painfully capable of making reckless choices.
That matters.
Samson was not the sanitized hero we sometimes turn him into.
He was a judge raised up during a dark period in Israel's history. His birth had been announced before he was conceived. He was set apart from the womb. God's calling rested upon his life.
And yet Samson could be impulsive, angry, secretive, driven by appetite, and dangerously confident in his own strength.
That tension is part of the point.
God's power working through Samson never meant that everything Samson desired was righteous.
Spiritual gifting is not the same thing as spiritual maturity.
You can be strong in one place and frighteningly weak in another.
You can know Scripture and still have an appetite you refuse to surrender.
You can worship publicly and struggle privately.
You can have people admire what God has placed upon you while almost nobody knows what is slowly destroying you.
Maybe that sentence found you.
Samson went down toward Timnah because he had seen a Philistine woman he wanted to marry. His parents objected, asking why he would seek a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines.
Samson's response was essentially: get her for me, because she is right in my eyes.
That phrase should bother us.
Because Judges repeatedly describes an age in which people did what was right in their own eyes.
And Samson's eyes would become one of the recurring battlegrounds of his life.
He saw.
He wanted.
He pursued.
How many disasters still begin that way?
Not because something was right before God.
Because it looked right to us.
Then, somewhere near the vineyards of Timnah, everything changed.
Scripture says a young lion came roaring toward Samson.
No sword.
No spear.
No weapon in his hand.
Just Samson...
and the lion.
Then Judges 14:6 says:
“וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה”
Vattitzlach alav Ruach YHWH.
The sense is that the Spirit of the LORD rushed powerfully upon him.
That detail cannot be removed from the story.
Samson's victory is not presented merely as the achievement of an unusually muscular man.
The text points us toward the empowering presence of God.
Samson tore the lion apart with his bare hands.
And then he kept walking.
He did not even tell his father and mother what had happened.
Imagine carrying a victory nobody knows about.
Imagine surviving something privately that would have terrified everyone who knows you.
Some of you understand that better than you wish you did.
People see you smiling now.
They did not hear the roar.
They see you worshipping.
They never saw the night you nearly quit.
They see the marriage that survived.
They don't know how close it came to dying.
They see the person who serves Jesus today.
They don't know who you used to be when nobody was watching.
They see honey.
They never met the lion.
Time passed.
Then Samson returned along that road.
And this time, he deliberately turned aside to look at what remained of the animal he had killed.
Judges 14:8 records the strange discovery:
“וְהִנֵּה עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים בִּגְוִיַּת הָאַרְיֵה וּדְבָשׁ”
Vehinneh adat devorim bigviyyat ha'aryeh udevash.
In plain sense:
Behold, a swarm of bees was in the body of the lion—and honey.
Honey.
Inside the remains of what once tried to kill him.
Read that again slowly.
The place associated with terror now contained sweetness.
The thing that once came roaring against him had become the location of something he could eat.
The predator was dead.
And inside its remains was honey.
Now we must be careful here.
Judges does not explicitly tell us, “The lion symbolizes your trials,” nor does it say, “The honey symbolizes salvation.” We should never force Scripture to say what Scripture does not say.
The immediate story explains Samson's coming riddle.
But the image is so striking that it can legitimately remind Christians of a truth proclaimed throughout the rest of Scripture:
God is astonishingly capable of bringing good out of places marked by suffering, evil, weakness, judgment, and death without ever calling evil good.
Joseph could tell the brothers who betrayed him that they intended evil against him, while God intended it for good.
Paul could write that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And at the very center of Christianity stands an even greater scandal:
a cross.
Rome meant it for execution.
Human wickedness nailed the innocent Son of God there.
Yet through that very death, according to God's redemptive purpose, came forgiveness and reconciliation for sinners.
That does not mean your suffering was good.
It means suffering does not get the final word when your life belongs to God.
That betrayal was not good.
The abuse was not good.
The addiction was not good.
Your sin was not good.
The funeral was not good.
The divorce papers were not good.
The diagnosis was not good.
The night you broke down on the bathroom floor was not good.
The years you wasted running from God were not good.
Christianity does not require us to rename darkness and call it light.
It announces something far more breathtaking:
darkness cannot defeat the redemptive purposes of God.
Samson reached into the remains and took honey.
Later, at his wedding feast, he turned what had happened into a riddle.
The Hebrew of Judges 14:14 is compact and unforgettable:

“מֵהָאֹכֵל יָצָא מַאֲכָל
וּמֵעַז יָצָא מָתוֹק”

Meha'okhel yatza ma'akhal,
ume'az yatza matok.

“Out of the eater came something to eat,
and out of the strong came something sweet.”
The eater became the source of food.
The strong became the place of sweetness.
Nobody could solve it.
Of course they couldn't.
They had not seen what Samson had seen.
They didn't know about the lion.
They didn't know about the battle.
They didn't know about the carcass.
They didn't know where the honey came from.
And there are people looking at your life right now who cannot understand your worship because they don't know what God brought you through.
They don't understand why you cry when you sing about grace.
They don't know what you were forgiven of.
They don't know how close you came to destroying everything.
They don't know the secret prayer God answered.
They don't know the temptation you fought at 2:00 in the morning.
They don't know the hospital corridor.
They don't know the betrayal.
They don't know the grave you stood beside.
They don't know how far you wandered.
They don't know the lion.
So they cannot understand why the honey tastes so sweet.
But you know.
And God knows.
Yet there is another side to Samson's story that we cannot romanticize.
The same man who killed a lion could not consistently master his own appetites.
That may be the most frightening part.
He could defeat something outside himself while slowly losing battles inside himself.
He could tear apart a lion but repeatedly allow desire, anger, pride, secrecy, and compromised relationships to pull him toward destruction.
And if we're courageous enough to admit it, Samson can look painfully familiar.
Some of us are incredibly good at fighting visible lions.
We work.
Provide.
Lead.
Preach.
Serve.
Protect.
Build.
Survive.
Everybody calls us strong.
But there is another battle.
The browser history.
The bitterness.
The secret messages.
The bottle.
The jealousy.
The obsession.
The pride.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from God.
The habit you keep renaming so you don't have to call it sin.
The wound you have turned into permission to hurt everybody around you.
The applause you secretly need.
The anger your family has learned to walk around.
You can kill lions in public and still be dying in private.
Samson's strength never made Samson his own savior.
And yours won't either.

Eventually the riddle itself became entangled in manipulation, threats, betrayal, rage, and bloodshed. Samson's life continued spiraling through extraordinary victories and devastating compromises until the man famous for his eyes eventually lost them.
The hero became a prisoner.
The strong man became entertainment for his enemies.
The man who once tore apart a lion was eventually led by the hand.
That is where cheap motivational Christianity would abandon Samson.
God didn't.
Near the end of Samson's story, blind and humiliated, he prayed again.
And God heard him.
Samson's story is messy enough that Hebrews 11 later mentioning him among people associated with faith can surprise us.
Because grace has always been scandalous.
Not cheap.
Not permissive.
Not indifferent to sin.
Scandalous.
Grace does not tell Samson that his choices did not matter.
They mattered terribly.
Grace does not erase consequences.
Grace means human failure does not possess greater authority than the mercy and purposes of God.
And this is where Samson's strange riddle can turn our eyes toward Someone infinitely greater than Samson.
Jesus Christ.
Samson killed a lion and later found sweetness associated with its death.
Jesus did something incomparably greater.
He entered death itself.
Not because death overpowered Him as an unwilling victim, but because He willingly laid down His life for sinners.
At Calvary, humanity's darkest crime became the stage upon which God's saving purpose was accomplished.
The cross looked like defeat.
Then came Sunday.
The tomb looked final.
Then the stone was rolled away.
Death swallowed countless generations.
Then Christ rose.
The eater was defeated.
The grave did not get the final word.
And because Jesus lives, repentance is not the funeral of your hope.
It is where resurrection life begins.
You may have done things you cannot undo.
You may carry consequences you cannot erase.
You may have wasted years.
You may have betrayed people.
You may have compromised.
You may have been the victim in one chapter and the villain in another.
You may be reading this while hiding something from everybody who loves you.
But listen carefully:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make respectable people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
Real ones.
Guilty ones.
Ashamed ones.
Addicted ones.
Religious ones.
Broken ones.
Proud ones.
People with carcasses in their past.
People who still hear lions roaring in their memories.
People like Samson.
People like us.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.

The Gospel is that your sin mattered so much that Christ bore judgment for sinners upon the cross, and God's grace is so astonishing that everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Maybe the lion in your story has already fallen.
Maybe you're still fighting it.
Maybe, if you're honest, you have discovered that the most dangerous lion was never outside you.
It was the sin within.
Either way, your answer is not Samson's strength.
Your answer is Samson's God.
Your answer is Jesus.
So stop pretending.
Stop polishing the testimony while hiding the wound.
Stop calling bondage a personality trait.
Stop defending what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Bring it into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Return.
Ask for help.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Walk into church again.
Tell a mature believer the truth.
Come back to Christ.
There is grace for the prodigal who turns home.
And maybe one day you will stand in a place you once thought would destroy you and realize:
the lion did not write the ending.
Jesus did.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't write an impressive comment.
Write an honest one.
You don't have to tell strangers every detail.
God already knows the whole story.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the moment hiding begins to lose its power.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't ignore that.
Send it privately to the person who thinks their worst chapter disqualified them from God's mercy.
Send it to the believer who wandered.
Send it to the person who doesn't believe yet but needs to understand what Christians actually mean by grace.
Not because every day will feel spiritual, but because there may come a night when the lion starts roaring again and you need to remember that the roar is not the same thing as the ending.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you open Scripture, confront sin, return to prayer, understand grace, or look toward Jesus again, stay close.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves someone is a better Christian.
It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is the gift of God through Christ.
But generosity can be one practical way believers choose to glorify God by helping sound biblical encouragement reach more people.
It is mission.
It is helping another exhausted believer encounter Scripture.
Helping another prodigal remember the road home.
Helping another person discover that Christianity is not about pretending to be strong enough.
It is about discovering that Christ is enough.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Forgive someone.
Confess something.
Return somewhere.
Repent of something.
Pray for someone.
Because Samson's riddle was never merely interesting because honey appeared inside a dead lion.
It was unforgettable because nobody looking at the sweetness could understand it without knowing the story of the battle.
Maybe people won't understand your worship either.
Let them wonder.
You know where Jesus found you.
You know what should have destroyed you.
You know what you deserved.
You know the roar.
You know the scars.
And if Christ has redeemed you...
you know why grace tastes so sweet.
The lion may explain your scars. But it does not get to write your ending. Jesus does.
